orchestrator_output.reformulated_query: Overview and administration of the Chola dynasty in medieval India
orchestrator_output.text_narration: The Chola Dynasty was one of the longest-ruling and most powerful dynasties in southern India, flourishing mainly between the 9th and 13th centuries CE. Centered around the fertile Kaveri River delta in Tamil Nadu, the Cholas created a vast empire known for its military power, naval strength, splendid temples, and democratic village governance. The Chola empire reached its peak under two famous rulers, Rajaraja the First and his son Rajendra the First. Rajaraja built a powerful navy, conquered parts of Sri Lanka, and established control over trade routes in the Indian Ocean. His son Rajendra extended the empire further north up to the Ganga river and led successful naval expeditions against the Sri Vijaya kingdom in South-East Asia. A unique feature of Chola rule was its highly efficient local administration and self-governing village assemblies. The empire was divided into provinces called Mandalams, which were further split into districts called Valanadus and Nadus. At the village level, two types of assemblies functioned: Ur for general peasant villages, and Sabha for Brahmin landholder settlements, where members were elected by lottery through palm leaf slips. Chola temples were not just places of worship, but also vibrant hubs of economic, social, and cultural life. Craftsmen made intricate bronze sculptures, with the dancing Nataraja figure being world-famous. Lands were gifted to temples, supporting priests, dancers, musicians, and artisans, making temple towns prosperous centers of medieval society.
